a: Ramoth-gilead
p: The war that killed Ahab at Ramoth-gilead is still going on twelve years later, now against Hazael.
b: Ramoth-gilead, a fortress east of the Jordan, was where Ahab died fighting the Arameans (1 Kings 22:29–37). Under his son Joram, Israel holds the town against Hazael, the new king of Aram, whom Elisha had foreseen as Israel's scourge (8:12–15, 8:28–29). The army is camped there and its commanders are together, which is why a coup can begin there. The scene is set in about 841 BC.

a: Jehu son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi
p: Jehu is "son of Nimshi" in 1 Kings 19:16, but here Nimshi is his grandfather. Assyria called him "son of Omri."
b: Hebrew ben, "son," can mean grandson or descendant, so "son of Nimshi" in 1 Kings 19:16 and 2 Kings 9:20 is a family name, while Jehoshaphat (not the king of Judah) was his father. The Assyrian scribes of Shalmaneser III called him "Jehu son of Omri" (see the note on 10:34). That almost certainly means "Jehu of the house of Omri," the Assyrian name for Israel, though a few scholars have taken it literally and argued that Jehu belonged to a side branch of Omri's family.

a: I anoint you as king over Israel
p: At Horeb, God told Elijah to anoint Jehu. Elijah never did; his successor's disciple does it in a back room.
b: At Mount Horeb the LORD gave Elijah three tasks: anoint Hazael over Aram, Jehu over Israel, and Elisha as prophet (1 Kings 19:15–16): "Jehu son of Nimshi you are to anoint as king over Israel" (1 Kings 19:16). Elijah called Elisha, but the other two were left to the next generation: Elisha told Hazael he would be king (8:13), and now he sends a young prophet to anoint Jehu. Like Samuel anointing David among his brothers (1 Samuel 16:13), the act is private and dangerous, and the messenger runs as soon as it is done.

a: the young man, the prophet's young man
p: The Hebrew says "the young man, the young man the prophet." Jewish tradition named him: Jonah son of Amittai.
b: The repeated hanna'ar hanna'ar may be a copying slip (one "young man" written twice) or a way of saying "the young man, the prophet's servant." The Plain keeps both. The messenger is unnamed, but the ancient Jewish chronicle Seder Olam and Rashi identify him as Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet of 14:25 and of the book of Jonah. Nothing in Kings says so, but it ties together two prophets who announce good news to northern kings.

a: the blood of my servants the prophets
p: Jezebel had killed the LORD's prophets. The anointing makes Jehu the instrument of their vengeance.
b: Jezebel was "wiping out the prophets of the LORD" (1 Kings 18:4; compare 1 Kings 18:13), and Elijah complained that he alone was left (1 Kings 19:10). The phrase echoes the Song of Moses, where the Hebrew text says God will avenge the blood of his servants (Deuteronomy 32:43; this site's Plain there follows the Qumran and Greek reading, "his sons' blood"), and Revelation takes it up when God judges the city drunk with the blood of the saints and prophets (Revelation 19:2), in the same book where a false prophet in Thyatira is called "Jezebel" (Revelation 2:20). Whether Jehu's way of carrying out this vengeance pleased God is a question the Bible itself raises (see the note on 10:30).
r: 1 Kings 18:4; 1 Kings 18:13; 1 Kings 19:10; Deuteronomy 32:43; Revelation 2:20; Revelation 19:2

a: every male of Ahab's, the bound and the free
p: The words repeat what was said against Jeroboam's house and Ahab's house. Literally, "one who urinates against a wall."
b: The prophet repeats, nearly word for word, Elijah's sentence on Ahab (1 Kings 21:21–22), which itself repeats the sentence on Jeroboam (1 Kings 14:10) and Baasha (1 Kings 16:3–4). The coarse Hebrew idiom for males, "one who pisses against a wall" in the KJV, belongs to this curse formula (1 Samuel 25:22). "Bound and free" probably means everyone, whatever his standing, though its exact sense is debated (see 14:26 and Deuteronomy 32:36). Kings tells the fall of each northern dynasty with the same words, so that the reader sees a pattern of judgment.

a: that madman
p: The officers call the prophet meshugga, a madman. Jehu himself will soon be said to drive "like a madman."
b: The word meshugga (from which Yiddish and English get "meshuggah") is used of prophets by people who scorn them (Jeremiah 29:26; Hosea 9:7), and of David faking madness (1 Samuel 21:15). Prophets sometimes acted in strange ways, and the army men take it for granted that this one is unhinged. The narrator plays on the word: in 9:20 the watchman says Jehu drives beshigga'on, "with madness." The "madman" anoints a mad driver, and the reader is left to judge which madness is from God.

a: laid it down under him on the steps themselves
p: Spreading cloaks under a new king was a sign of homage. The word for the steps is literally "the bone of the stairs."
b: Gerem means "bone," and so "the self" or "the very" thing; "the bone of the steps" may mean the bare steps, the top step, or the steps themselves. Whatever the sense, the officers make a rough throne out of a stairway and their own cloaks, blow the ram's horn and shout the formula used for a new king (2 Samuel 15:10; 1 Kings 1:39). Readers of the gospels think of the crowds spreading their cloaks on the road before Jesus as he rode into Jerusalem as king (Matthew 21:8; Luke 19:36).

a: to be healed
p: 8:28–29 already told this. The repetition picks up the story where the Ahaziah account left it.
b: This verse repeats almost word for word what 8:28–29 said: Joram was wounded at Ramoth-gilead and went home to Jezreel to recover, and Ahaziah came to visit him. Repeating a summary like this is a common way for a Hebrew narrator to resume a story after a side scene. It also explains why both kings are in Jezreel, away from the army, at the very moment the army turns against them.

a: King Jehoram
p: Israel's king is "Joram" in 9:14 and "Jehoram" in 9:15. The two forms are one name.
b: Yoram and Yehoram are a short and a long form of one name, "the LORD is high." In these years both kingdoms had a king by that name: Joram son of Ahab in Israel and Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat in Judah, who married Ahab's daughter Athaliah (8:16–18). The Hebrew uses both forms for both kings (8:16–29; 9:14–24; 11:2; 12:18). The Plain follows the form in each verse. The notes and topic pages call Israel's king Joram and Judah's Jehoram, as many English versions do, to tell them apart. The same holds for Joash and Jehoash (see the note on 12:1).

a: Is it peace?
p: "Peace" (shalom) comes up nine times in this chapter. Each time, there is no peace.
b: Hashalom? is the ordinary Hebrew greeting-question, "Is all well?" or "Do you come in peace?" The servants ask it of Jehu (9:11), Joram's riders ask it (9:17–19), Joram asks it (9:22), and Jezebel throws it at Jehu in mockery (9:31). Jehu's answers turn it around: "Peace? What is that to you?" and "What peace is there?" The Plain keeps the one word "peace" throughout so that the reader can hear the drumbeat. Elijah's word against Ahab's house had promised no peace, and the chapter shows it.

a: He drives like a madman
p: Jehu was known for the way he drove. The word picks up the "madman" of 9:11.
b: The watchman can recognize Jehu by his driving before he can see his face: he drives beshigga'on, "in madness," from the same root as meshugga, "madman" (9:11). The KJV's "furiously" has made "a Jehu" an English nickname for a reckless driver since the seventeenth century. The point in the story is speed and boldness: Jehu does not stop to answer the riders but sweeps them into his column.

a: her prostitution and her many sorceries
p: The words are the prophets' language for idolatry, not a report that Jezebel was literally a prostitute or a witch.
b: "Prostitution" (zenunim) is the prophets' standard picture of worshiping other gods, as unfaithfulness to the LORD, Israel's husband (Hosea 1:2; Hosea 2:2; Ezekiel 16). "Sorceries" (keshafim) are magic practices that the Law forbids (Deuteronomy 18:10). Nahum pairs the same two words against Nineveh (Nahum 3:4). Jehu's charge is that Jezebel's Baal worship has corrupted the land; nothing in Kings says she sold herself or practiced witchcraft in the modern sense. Revelation uses "Jezebel" as a name for a teacher who leads believers into "sexual sin" and idolatry (Revelation 2:20).
r: Hosea 1:2; Hosea 2:2; Nahum 3:4; Deuteronomy 18:10; 1 Kings 16:31–33; Revelation 2:20

a: shot Jehoram between the arms
p: An Aramaic victory stone found at Tel Dan seems to say that the king of Aram, not Jehu, killed both kings.
b: In 1993–94 fragments of a stone inscription were found at Tel Dan in northern Israel. Its speaker, almost certainly Hazael of Aram, boasts that he killed "[Jeho]ram son of [Ahab], king of Israel" and "[Ahaz]iahu son of [Jehoram, kin]g of the house of David." The names are partly restored. Most scholars accept them, but Athas disputes how the fragments fit together, dates the stone later (to Hazael's son, about 796 BC) and reads it differently. How does this fit Kings? (1) Hazael may claim credit for deaths caused by his war, since Joram was wounded fighting him (9:15). (2) Jehu may have acted as Hazael's ally or agent, so that Hazael counted the deaths as his. (3) Kings may give Jehu credit that was not his. (4) The stone may exaggerate. It is also the earliest mention of the "house of David" (bytdwd) outside the Bible; early doubts about that reading (Lemche, Davies) are now a minority view.

a: the LORD laid this heavy word on him
p: The word for oracle, massa, means "something lifted," a load. The LORD "lifted" this load on Ahab.
b: Massa is the title of many prophetic oracles of judgment (Isaiah 13:1; Nahum 1:1), and the KJV renders it "burden." It comes from nasa, "to lift," and Jehu uses both words together: the LORD "lifted this lifting on him." Jehu claims he was there, riding behind Ahab, when Elijah met the king in Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21:17–24). Kings never says that before; it makes Jehu a witness of the oracle he now carries out.

a: the blood of his sons
p: 1 Kings 21 mentions only Naboth. Jehu adds that his sons were killed too, and that payment will come on that plot.
b: In 1 Kings 21:13 Naboth is stoned; his sons are not mentioned. If they were killed as well, no heir was left to claim the vineyard, and the crown could take it. Jehu's quotation of the oracle differs from 1 Kings 21:19, which spoke of dogs licking Ahab's blood where they licked Naboth's. Prophetic words are often quoted freely in Kings. Here the sentence lands not on Ahab, who died in Samaria (1 Kings 22:37–38), but on his son, as 1 Kings 21:29 had said it would: "In his son's lifetime I will bring the disaster on his house."

a: He fled to Megiddo and died there
p: Kings has Ahaziah shot near Ibleam, dying at Megiddo. Chronicles has him found hiding in Samaria.
b: Chronicles says of Ahaziah, "He was caught hiding in Samaria, and they brought him to Jehu and put him to death" (2 Chronicles 22:9), and it says they buried him out of respect for his grandfather Jehoshaphat, without saying where. The two accounts are hard to fit together. Harmonizers suggest that he fled first to Samaria and then north, or that Chronicles compresses events. Critical scholars think Chronicles used a different tradition or retold the story to stress that his downfall was "God's doing" (2 Chronicles 22:7). The Tel Dan stele adds a third voice, crediting Hazael (see the note on 9:24).

a: in the eleventh year of Joram
p: 8:25 dated Ahaziah's accession to Joram's twelfth year. Here it is the eleventh.
b: Kings gives both figures, and scholars usually explain them by two ways of counting a king's first year. If the year a king took the throne counted as his first year ("non-accession" dating), the same moment could be "year twelve" in one system and "year eleven" in the other. Thiele argued that Israel and Judah used different systems at different times; others think one figure came from a different source. Either way, Ahaziah reigned only about a year (8:26). See the topic "Dating the Kings."

a: she put paint around her eyes and dressed her hair
t: Why did Jezebel paint her eyes?
p: Popular belief says she tried to seduce Jehu. The text does not say so; many see a queen dressing for death.
b: Puk is black eye paint, made from antimony or galena, used by women across the ancient Near East (Jeremiah 4:30; Ezekiel 23:40; Job's daughter Keren-happuch, "horn of eye paint," Job 42:14). The phrase "painted Jezebel" has made her a byword for a seductress. But she is now a grandmother, and her first words are a taunt, not an invitation (9:31). Many scholars therefore read her makeup and headdress as royal dignity: she meets her killer as a queen, at the palace window where royal women appeared in Near Eastern art. Others see vanity or a last bid to keep power. The text records the act and leaves the motive open.

a: Is it peace, Zimri, who killed his master?
p: Zimri killed his king and reigned seven days before dying in flames. Jezebel's taunt predicts the same for Jehu.
b: Zimri, a chariot commander, murdered King Elah and wiped out Baasha's house, then lasted only seven days before Omri besieged him and he burned the palace down over himself (1 Kings 16:9–20). Omri, Jezebel's father-in-law, was the man who brought Zimri down. Calling Jehu "Zimri" is a bitter joke and a warning: usurpers do not last. The Hebrew says "his master," not "your master," which may make the line almost a proverb: "Zimri, the one who killed his master." Jehu's dynasty in fact lasted nearly a century.

a: court officials
p: Sarisim can mean eunuchs or simply royal officials. In a queen's household, eunuchs are likely.
b: The word saris comes from an Akkadian phrase meaning "one of the king's head," a courtier. In Assyria many such officials were eunuchs, and the word often carries that sense in the Bible (Isaiah 56:3–5), but it is also used of married officials such as Potiphar (Genesis 39:1). Servants of a queen were often eunuchs. Their quick switch of loyalty, at Jehu's "Who is with me?", decides Jezebel's end.

a: She was a king's daughter, after all
p: Jezebel was the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians. Even Jehu feels he must bury royalty.
b: 1 Kings 16:31 calls her the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians; Josephus, quoting Menander of Ephesus, makes Ithobaal a priest of Astarte who seized the throne of Tyre. Jehu calls her "this woman under a curse," yet orders burial out of respect for royal blood. In the ancient world, being left unburied was among the worst fates (Jeremiah 22:19). An ancient seal inscribed "YZBL," with royal Phoenician symbols, has been suggested as hers; the identification is possible but not proven.

a: On the land of Jezreel the dogs will eat Jezebel's flesh
p: 1 Kings 21:23 said, "The dogs will eat Jezebel by the rampart of Jezreel." Jehu quotes it in an expanded form.
b: Elijah's word was: "The dogs will eat Jezebel by the rampart of Jezreel" (1 Kings 21:23). Jehu's version (9:36–37) has "land" (chelek) instead of "rampart" (chel), which differ by one letter in Hebrew, and adds the picture of her corpse as manure and the line "No one will be able to say, 'This is Jezebel.'" Kings often lets characters quote prophecy loosely. Some scholars think the two forms reflect the same word reshaped in retelling; others read 1 Kings 21:23 as the older wording. The point is the same: the queen who had Naboth stoned is denied even a grave.

a: like manure spread on the open field
p: The image of corpses as dung on a field becomes a stock curse in the prophets, especially Jeremiah.
b: Domen is manure spread to fertilize a field. To lie unburied like dung is a curse for those under God's judgment (Psalm 83:10; Jeremiah 8:2; Jeremiah 9:22; Jeremiah 16:4; Jeremiah 25:33). For Jezebel the curse is complete: not even a name remains to mark her. The verse ends the chapter with the word the whole revolt has been about, "Jezebel," and with the claim that she will no longer be recognized.

a: Ahab had seventy sons
p: "Seventy sons" stands for the whole royal family, as with Gideon's seventy sons, murdered by Abimelech.
b: Seventy is a round number for a large, complete family: Jacob's household that went to Egypt (Genesis 46:27), Gideon's sons (Judges 8:30), Abdon's grandsons (Judges 12:14). The closest parallel is grim: Abimelech murdered his seventy brothers "on one stone" to seize power (Judges 9:5). "Sons" here likely includes grandsons and other male descendants of Ahab, raised by guardians among the nobles of Samaria.

a: take the heads of the men who are your master's sons
p: "Heads" in Hebrew can mean leaders or literal heads. Jehu's letter is written so that the killing falls on others.
b: Rashe, "heads of," is a common way to say "chiefs, leaders" (Exodus 18:25). Jehu's order could mean "bring the leading men of your master's sons" or "bring their heads." The nobles of Samaria take it the second way and kill all seventy. The next morning Jehu can tell the crowd, "I killed him. But all these, who struck them down?" (10:9). Many commentators see a calculated ambiguity: the men who might have resisted Jehu are now his accomplices.

a: Make two heaps of them by the gate entrance
p: Assyrian kings boasted of piling enemy heads at city gates. Jehu stages the same terror in Jezreel.
b: The Assyrian annals of Ashurnasirpal II and Shalmaneser III, Jehu's contemporaries, describe piles of heads set up before conquered cities, and palace reliefs show soldiers stacking them. A gate was the town's public square, where elders sat and everyone passed (Ruth 4:1). Displaying the heads there overnight announced that Ahab's line was finished and warned anyone who might think otherwise.

a: You are in the right
p: "You are righteous" can mean "you are innocent" or "you be the judge." Either way, Jehu shares out the guilt.
b: Tsaddiqim 'attem literally says "You are righteous." Read as "You are innocent," Jehu reassures the crowd that they bear no blame for Joram's death. Read as "You are fair-minded, judge for yourselves," he invites them to see that more than one hand was involved. Either way, his speech makes the nobles' massacre part of God's plan (10:10). Some readers admire his frankness; many modern scholars see skilled political spin, and note that the Bible lets readers see it.

a: will drop to the ground
p: A word that "falls to the ground" fails. Jehu claims that every word against Ahab's house has come true.
b: The idiom is used of Samuel, whose words the LORD let none "fall to the ground" (1 Samuel 3:19), and of God's promises to Israel, none of which fell (Joshua 21:45; 1 Kings 8:56). Kings counts the fulfilled prophecies carefully, and Jehu presents himself as their fulfillment. His appeal to Elijah also gives a usurper legitimacy. See also 9:36 and 10:17.

a: the brothers of Ahaziah king of Judah
p: Chronicles says Ahaziah's brothers had already been killed. These men are his nephews or cousins.
b: 2 Chronicles 21:17 says raiders took all of Jehoram's sons except Ahaziah, and 2 Chronicles 22:8 calls Jehu's victims "the sons of Ahaziah's brothers." Hebrew "brothers" often means kinsmen. These forty-two princes of Judah were on a family visit to Jezreel and to "the queen mother," Jezebel, whose fate they did not know. Their deaths, together with Ahaziah's, nearly wiped out David's line and gave Athaliah her chance (11:1).

a: Jehonadab son of Rechab
p: Jehonadab is the ancestor of the Rechabites, who lived in tents and drank no wine, as Jeremiah 35 describes.
b: About 240 years later Jeremiah tests the Rechabites by offering them wine. They refuse, because their ancestor "Jonadab son of Rechab" commanded them never to drink wine, build houses, sow seed or plant vineyards, but to live in tents (Jeremiah 35:6–10). God holds up their loyalty as a rebuke to Judah. Their link to the Kenites is suggested by 1 Chronicles 2:55. Jehonadab's presence in Jehu's chariot gives the revolt the backing of a strict, old-fashioned party of the LORD's followers.

a: Jehonadab said, "It is." "If it is, give me your hand."
p: The Hebrew reads "There is, and there is. Give your hand." Most translators split the words between two speakers.
b: Jehu asks, "Is your heart straight?" and the Hebrew answer is yesh va-yesh, "there is, and there is," followed by "Give your hand." Read as it stands, Jehonadab answers emphatically, "It is, it is!" and Jehu (or Jehonadab) says, "Give your hand." The Greek translation adds "and Jehu said," giving "It is." "If it is, give me your hand," and the KJV and most modern versions read it the same way. The Plain follows that division, which needs only a small change in how the words are read, but the meaning is the same either way.
orig: יֵשׁ וָיֵשׁ תְּנָה אֶת־יָדֶךָ (yesh vayesh tenah 'et-yadekha)

a: watch how zealous I am for the LORD
p: Jehu claims the zeal of Phinehas and Elijah. Whether his zeal was for God or for himself is debated from Hosea onward.
b: "Zeal" (qin'ah) for the LORD was the mark of Phinehas, who killed an Israelite and a Midianite woman to stop a plague (Numbers 25:11–13), and of Elijah, who said, "I have burned with zeal for the LORD" (1 Kings 19:10, 19:14). Jehu claims to stand in that line. Kings records that God approved what he did to Ahab's house (10:30), but also that he kept Jeroboam's calves (10:29–31). Jewish and Christian interpreters, from the rabbis to Calvin, have often said that his zeal was real but mixed with ambition. Later Jewish "zealots" looked to Phinehas, not Jehu, as their model.

a: Jehu was playing a trick
p: Jehu lies to trap Baal's worshipers. The rabbis said his false words came back to bind him.
b: Kings says plainly that Jehu acted "with cunning" ('oqbah, from the root of Jacob's name, the heel-grabber). The Bible tells other deceptions in war or crisis without comment (Joshua 2; 1 Samuel 16:2). The Talmud, though, reads 10:18 closely: Jehu said, "Jehu will serve him a great deal," and the rabbis taught that "a covenant is made with the lips," so that his pretended vow to serve Baal became real when he went on serving Jeroboam's calves (Bavli Sanhedrin 102a). Christian moral writers have used the scene to debate whether deceit can ever serve God.

a: Set apart a festival assembly for Baal
t: A parody of a holy day
p: 'Atsarah is the word for the LORD's festival assemblies. Jehu proclaims one for Baal, as bait.
b: An 'atsarah is the closing gathering of a feast (Leviticus 23:36; Deuteronomy 16:8) or a fast called in a crisis (Joel 1:14; Joel 2:15). To "set it apart" (qaddeshu, "make holy") is the language of Israel's worship. Jehu borrows it for Baal so that every worshiper will feel bound to come. The prophet Amos would later say the LORD hates Israel's own 'atsarot when they go with injustice (Amos 5:21).

a: Bring out clothes for everyone who serves Baal
p: Worshipers in Baal's house wore special garments. Here the robes also mark them out for slaughter.
b: Ancient temples kept vestments for priests and sometimes for worshipers (Genesis 35:2; Zephaniah 1:8 speaks of "foreign clothing"). In Jehu's plan, the robes have a second use: anyone dressed for Baal is a target, and Jehu's search for "servants of the LORD" in the crowd (10:23) makes sure no one else is caught. The irony is sharp: the worshipers are carefully kept pure for their god, and then killed.

a: the runners and the officers
p: The "runners" were the royal bodyguard, so called from running before the king's chariot.
b: Ratsim, "runners," are the king's guard (1 Samuel 22:17; 1 Kings 1:5; 1 Kings 14:27–28), named for their duty of running before his chariot. The same guard will crown Joash in 11:4–19. The "officers" (shalishim) are literally "third men," probably the third man in a chariot, later a title for senior aides (see Bidkar in 9:25 and Pekah in 15:25).

a: the stronghold of the house of Baal
t: "The city of the house of Baal"
p: The Hebrew says "the city of the house of Baal": an inner stronghold, or a slip for "inner sanctuary."
b: 'Ir usually means "city," but it can mean a fortified part of a city (2 Samuel 5:7: "Zion's fortress. It is the City of David"). Here it may be a walled inner precinct of the temple. Many scholars think the text first read devir, "inner sanctuary," the word for the temple's most holy room (1 Kings 6:5), and several modern translations render it that way. The Plain keeps the Hebrew and gives it the sense "stronghold."

a: carried the standing stones out of the house of Baal and burned it
p: Stone pillars do not burn. Some versions read one "pillar"; some scholars think a wooden Asherah was burned.
b: The Hebrew has "pillars" (plural) but "burned it" (singular). A matsevah is normally a standing stone (Genesis 28:18), which would be smashed, as in 10:27, not burned. The Greek and the Latin read the singular, "the pillar" (see the variant), and many scholars suggest the burned object was an Asherah pole, the wooden cult symbol often found with standing stones (Deuteronomy 7:5; 1 Kings 14:23), or a wooden pillar. Deuteronomy commands both: "Shatter their standing stones. Burn their Asherah poles with fire" (Deuteronomy 12:3).

a: turned it into toilets
t: A temple made into a latrine
p: The written Hebrew says "latrines"; the reading tradition substitutes a politer word, "places of going out."
b: The consonants spell machara'ot, from the word for dung; the Masoretes marked it to be read motsa'ot, "outlets" or "privies," a euphemism, as they did with other coarse words (compare 18:27). The meaning is the same either way: Baal's house was turned into a public toilet, the deepest insult possible to a sacred place, and it was still one "to this day," when the account was written.

a: the gold calves that stood at Bethel and at Dan
p: Jehu destroyed Baal but kept the calf shrines, which were Israel's state religion and served his politics.
b: Jeroboam set up the gold calves at Bethel and Dan to keep his people from going to Jerusalem (1 Kings 12:26–30). Kings treats them as the original sin of the northern kingdom and judges every northern king by them. Jehu's purge was aimed at Baal, the foreign god of Ahab's house; the calves were worship of the LORD in a form Kings rejects, and they were tied to Israel's independence from Judah. Removing them would have weakened Jehu's own throne. The pattern repeats in every reign that follows (13:2, 13:11, 14:24).

a: You did a good thing when you did what is right in my eyes
p: Kings has God praise Jehu. A century later Hosea announces punishment on Jehu's house "for the blood of Jezreel."
b: The LORD rewards Jehu with four generations on the throne, and Kings sees his revolt as the fulfillment of Elijah's word. Yet the prophet Hosea names his son Jezreel, "In a very little while I will bring the blood shed at Jezreel down on the house of Jehu, and I will put an end to the kingdom of the house of Israel" (Hosea 1:4). Readers have answered in several ways: (1) Jehu did God's will but with selfish motives or excess, such as killing Ahaziah and the princes of Judah, so the same acts were obedience and crime (Calvin on Hosea 1:4 and many others); (2) his later sins, above all keeping the calves, made his earlier bloodshed count as murder (Rashi and Radak on Hosea 1:4); (3) "the blood of Jezreel" means the dynasty's whole record of violence; (4) Hosea simply judges differently from Kings, and the Bible keeps both voices.

a: down to the fourth generation
p: The promise is kept: Jehoahaz, Jehoash, Jeroboam II and Zechariah. Then the dynasty ends (15:12).
b: Jehu's line produced Israel's longest dynasty: Jehu (about 841–814 BC), Jehoahaz, Jehoash, Jeroboam II and Zechariah, who was murdered after six months, about 753 BC. Kings marks the end with an explicit note that "so came true the word the LORD had spoken to Jehu" (15:12). The promise is generous and limited at once, a reward that also sets an end.

a: the LORD began to cut away pieces of Israel
p: Hazael took Israel's land east of the Jordan. Amos remembered Aram threshing Gilead with iron sledges.
b: With Shalmaneser III busy elsewhere after 838 BC, Hazael made Aram the strongest power in the region. He took Gilead and Bashan (10:33), pressed into Israel (13:3, 13:7) and reached Philistia and Jerusalem (12:17–18). Amos looks back: "they threshed Gilead with sledges of iron" (Amos 1:3). Elisha had wept when he foresaw it (8:12). The Tel Dan stele, if it is Hazael's, boasts of victories over Israel and Judah in the same years. Kings reads it as the LORD trimming a disobedient kingdom.

a: all his strength
p: Kings says nothing of it, but Assyria recorded Jehu's tribute in 841 BC and carved a picture of him or his envoy bowing.
b: The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III, found at Nimrud in 1846 and now in the British Museum, has a panel showing a bearded man kneeling with his face to the ground before the Assyrian king. The caption calls it "the tribute of Jehu (Ia-ú-a), son of Omri," and lists silver, gold, gold bowls and vessels, tin and a royal staff. Shalmaneser's annals place it in his eighteenth year, 841 BC, the year of Jehu's revolt. It is the only known picture of an Israelite or Judean king, or his envoy, from his own lifetime. Kings mentions Jehu's "strength" but not his bowing to Assyria.

a: twenty-eight years
p: Jehu's accession in 841 BC is one of the firmest dates in the chronology of the kings, thanks to the Assyrian record.
b: Because Shalmaneser received Jehu's tribute in his eighteenth year (841 BC), and Ahab fought him at Qarqar in his sixth (853 BC), the twelve years between fit the reigns of Ahaziah (two years, counted inclusively) and Joram (twelve). Nearly every system therefore dates Jehu's accession to 841 and his reign to about 841–814 BC (Thiele, Galil, Tadmor and Cogan). Albright's older system started him in 842. See the topic "Dating the Kings."

a: Athaliah, the mother of Ahaziah
t: Who was Athaliah, and why did she do it?
p: An Omride princess on David's throne. Kings calls her a usurper; some modern readers see a fight to survive.
b: Athaliah was the daughter of Ahab, or of Omri's house (8:18, 8:26), married to Jehoram of Judah to bind the two kingdoms together. In a few weeks Jehu had killed her son, her brother Joram, Jezebel, who was probably her mother, and forty-two princes of Judah. Kings presents her massacre of the royal family as pure ambition and does not count her six years with a regnal formula. Some modern scholars suggest she acted to save herself and the Omride party in Judah from Jehu's purge, and note that the narrator tells her story only from her enemies' side. No reading excuses killing her own grandchildren, if that is what "all the royal offspring" included.

a: wiped out all the royal offspring
p: God had promised David a lasting dynasty. For six years one hidden baby is all that is left of it.
b: The LORD promised that David's house would stand forever (2 Samuel 7:12–16) and that David would always have "a lamp" in Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:36; 1 Kings 15:4; 8:19). Athaliah's purge puts that promise in more danger than anything before the exile. The rescue of one infant from a massacre of royal children recalls Moses saved from Pharaoh's decree (Exodus 2:1–10), and Christian readers have compared it to the child Jesus escaping Herod (Matthew 2:13–16).

a: Jehosheba
p: Chronicles adds that Jehosheba was the wife of Jehoiada the priest. That explains how the boy could hide in the temple.
b: 2 Chronicles 22:11 calls her Jehoshabeath and adds that she was "the wife of Jehoiada the priest." As King Jehoram's daughter she was Ahaziah's sister, though perhaps by another mother than Athaliah. Her marriage into the priestly family explains how a royal baby could be hidden in the temple precinct for six years, and why Jehoiada becomes the leader of the coup. She is one of several women in Kings whose quiet courage changes the story.

a: the room where the beds were kept
p: The Hebrew is "the room of the beds," probably a storeroom for bedding and couches, where no one would look for a child.
b: Chadar hammittot, "the chamber of the beds," is usually rendered "bedroom." But a bedroom in the palace is a poor hiding place. Many commentators, ancient and modern, take it as a storeroom where beds and mattresses were kept. The child and his nurse were hidden there first, then moved to the temple (11:3).

a: the Carites
p: Probably mercenaries from Caria in Asia Minor, like the Cherethites and Pelethites who guarded David.
b: The Kari appear only here and in a Ketiv at 2 Samuel 20:23, where the reading tradition has "Cherethites." Most scholars identify them as Carians, a people of southwest Asia Minor famous as hired soldiers; Herodotus tells how Carian and Ionian mercenaries served the pharaohs of Egypt (Herodotus 2.152–154). A foreign bodyguard, loyal to the crown rather than to any faction, fits the palace guard of a king of Judah.

a: the ones who come in on the Sabbath
t: A coup timed to the Sabbath
p: Guard units changed shifts on the Sabbath. Jehoiada uses the moment when both the old and the new shifts are on hand.
b: The plan seems to be that on the Sabbath, when one shift came on duty and the other went off, Jehoiada could keep both at the temple and have twice the usual guard without raising alarm (11:9). The passage is one of the few pictures of the Sabbath before the exile (see also 4:23; Amos 8:5; Isaiah 1:13). In Chronicles the guards become Levites, and only priests and Levites enter the temple (2 Chronicles 23:4–8).

a: in shifts
p: The last word, massach, occurs nowhere else. Guesses: "in turns," "as a barrier," "to keep out."
b: Massach has been explained from a root meaning "to drive off" ("keep anyone from breaking in," as in the KJV's "that it be not broken down"), or as a word for a rotation or for a barrier. Some scholars think it is a copying error. The general sense is clear enough: the three detachments together sealed off the palace and the temple.

a: King David's spear and shields
p: Arming the guard with David's own weapons made the coronation a return of David's line.
b: David had brought gold shields taken from Hadadezer's officers to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 8:7), and Goliath's sword was kept at the sanctuary of Nob (1 Samuel 21:9). Whatever these particular weapons were, putting them in the guards' hands was a powerful sign: the boy-king they protect is David's heir, and the coup is a restoration, not a rebellion.

a: and the testimony
p: 'Edut may be a copy of God's law, a royal covenant document, or (with a small change) royal armlets.
b: Ha-'edut, "the testimony," usually refers to the Ten Words written on the tablets (Exodus 25:16). Here, given to a king at his coronation, it may be a copy of the law that the king was to keep with him (Deuteronomy 17:18–19), or a document of the covenant between God, king and people (11:17). Gerhard von Rad compared it to the Egyptian royal "protocol" with the king's throne names (Psalm 2:7). Others change one letter to read tse'adot, "armlets," since Saul's crown and armlet were brought to David (2 Samuel 1:10). The Plain keeps "testimony."

a: by the pillar, as kings did
t: The king's place by the pillar
p: Judah's kings had a set place "on" or "by" the pillar at the temple entrance, probably Jachin or Boaz.
b: Solomon set up two bronze pillars, Jachin and Boaz, at the temple porch (1 Kings 7:15–22). Josiah also stands "by the pillar" to make a covenant (23:3), and Ezekiel's prince has a fixed place at the gate (Ezekiel 46:2). Athaliah sees the boy standing where only a king stands, with the officers and trumpeters around him, and knows at once what has happened.

a: all the people of the land
p: In Kings, 'am ha'arets means Judah's landowning citizens. Later it came to mean the unlearned.
b: The "people of the land" appear at key moments in Judah's politics: they support Joash (11:14–20), put Josiah on the throne after his father's murder (21:24) and crown Jehoahaz (23:30). They seem to be the free landholders of Judah, loyal to David's house. Centuries later, in rabbinic Hebrew, 'am ha'arets meant a common person ignorant of the law, a sense that has misled some readers here.

a: where the horses come into the king's house
t: Claude's theory: two queens among the horses
p: My reading: both Omride queens die where horses go. The narrator may be pairing Athaliah's end with her mother's.
b: This is my own suggestion, though commentators have long noticed that chapters 9–11 form a unit. Jezebel is thrown down and her blood spatters "the horses" as Jehu tramples her (9:33). Athaliah, probably her daughter, is led out by "the road where the horses come into the king's house" and killed there. Both scenes take care to keep the sacred place clean: Jezebel dies at the palace, not in Baal's house; Athaliah is taken out so she will not be killed "in the LORD's house" (11:15). If the echo is deliberate, the two coups of 841 BC are told as one judgment on Ahab's house in both kingdoms.

a: Jehoiada made the covenant
p: Jehoiada renews the covenant between the LORD and his people, and also a covenant between king and people.
b: The first covenant binds king and people to be "a people belonging to the LORD," the language of Sinai (Exodus 19:5–6; Deuteronomy 26:17–18). The second binds king and people to each other, like the covenant the elders of Israel made with David at Hebron (2 Samuel 5:3). Scholars see here an early form of the covenant renewals of Josiah (23:1–3) and Ezra (Nehemiah 8–10), and a check on royal power: the king rules under God's covenant, not above it. Some critics think the first covenant was added by the Deuteronomistic editor.

a: Mattan, Baal's priest
t: A temple of Baal in Jerusalem
p: This is the only mention of a Baal temple in Jerusalem. Athaliah brought her family's religion with her.
b: Ahab built a house of Baal in Samaria (1 Kings 16:32). Kings now reveals a second in Jerusalem, presumably built under Athaliah, with a priest named Mattan ("gift," a common Phoenician name element). Chronicles adds that Athaliah's sons broke into the LORD's house and used its holy things for the Baals (2 Chronicles 24:7). The people of the land destroy it on the day of the coronation, as Jehu had destroyed Baal's house in Samaria (10:26–27).

a: Jehoash was seven years old when he became king
p: In Hebrew Bibles this verse is 12:1, so every verse of chapter 12 there is one number higher than in English Bibles.
b: English Bibles, following the Greek and Latin, end chapter 11 with Joash's age. The Hebrew text begins chapter 12 with it, so English 12:1–21 is Hebrew 12:2–22. Readers using a Jewish translation such as the JPS will find, for example, Hazael's attack on Gath at 12:18 rather than 12:17. This translation uses English numbering throughout.

a: he reigned in Jerusalem forty years
p: Forty is a round number, but Joash's long reign fits the chronologies: about 835–796 BC in Thiele's system.
b: Forty years recalls David and Solomon (1 Kings 2:11; 1 Kings 11:42) and may be rounded. Thiele dates Joash about 835–796 BC; other systems differ by a few years. His mother Zibiah ("gazelle") came from Beersheba, at Judah's southern edge, a reminder that the queen mother is named for almost every king of Judah (not for Jehoram or Ahaz) but for none of Israel's. The Hebrew calls this king both Jehoash (11:21–12:18) and Joash (12:19–20), and Israel's king of the same years both Joash and Jehoash. The Plain follows the form in each verse; the notes call Judah's king Joash and Israel's Jehoash to tell them apart.

a: all his days, since Jehoiada the priest had taught him
t: All his days, or only while Jehoiada lived?
p: "All his days, since Jehoiada taught him," or "all the days Jehoiada taught him"? Chronicles takes the latter.
b: The relative word 'asher can mean "that" ("all his days that Jehoiada instructed him") or "because." Chronicles reads it the first way: Joash did right "all the days of Jehoiada the priest" (2 Chronicles 24:2), and after Jehoiada's death he turned to the Asherah poles and had Jehoiada's son Zechariah stoned in the temple court. Zechariah's dying words were, "May the LORD see it, and may he seek it out" (2 Chronicles 24:22). Kings tells none of this. The Plain gives the reading that suits Kings on its own, with the Chronicles reading noted here.

a: the money that passes from each man in the count
p: The verse names three sources of income, each in obscure terms: a census payment, vow valuations and freewill gifts.
b: "Money that passes" (kesef 'over) may be ordinary currency (Genesis 23:16) or, more likely, the half-shekel paid in a census by "Everyone who crosses over to join those enrolled" (Exodus 30:13–14), with the same verb, the payment Chronicles calls "the tax of Moses" (2 Chronicles 24:6, 24:9). "Money for persons at the value set on each" refers to vows, where a person dedicated to God was redeemed at a fixed price (Leviticus 27:2–8). The third kind is freewill gifts. Some scholars think the first two phrases are glosses on one another.
orig: כֶּסֶף עוֹבֵר אִישׁ כֶּסֶף נַפְשׁוֹת עֶרְכּוֹ (kesef 'over 'ish kesef nafshot 'erko)

a: each one from those he knows
p: Makkar may mean a priest's acquaintance or patron, or a temple official who handled valuations.
b: The word appears only in this passage. One view takes it from nakar, "to recognize," so each priest collects from people he knows, the families who bring their offerings through him. Another links it to a word in texts from Ugarit for a merchant or assessor, so that "treasurer" is meant. Either way the system left money in the priests' hands, and the repairs did not happen (12:6).

a: one chest
p: Jehoiada's chest with a hole in its lid is the first collection box in the Bible.
b: Joash's chest became famous. Chronicles places it outside the temple gate and has the people bring "the tax of Moses" with joy (2 Chronicles 24:8–11). The Mishnah describes thirteen trumpet-shaped chests in the Second Temple for different offerings (Mishnah Shekalim 6:1, 6:5), and Jesus watched people putting money into such chests when a poor widow gave her two small coins (Mark 12:41–44). Josiah's repairs in 22:3–7 follow the same procedure, almost word for word.

a: the high priest
p: The title "the great priest" is rare before the exile. In Kings it appears only in the temple-repair stories.
b: Before the exile the chief priest is usually just "the priest" (11:9; 16:10). "The great priest" appears here and in the parallel stories of Josiah (22:4, 22:8; 23:4) in the law for priests (Leviticus 21:10) and in the laws of the cities of refuge (Numbers 35:25; Joshua 20:6). After the exile it becomes the normal title (Haggai 1:1). Some scholars think the phrase was updated by a later editor; others think the title simply was not often used.

a: to the masons and the stone cutters
p: A stone tablet describing Joash's repairs surfaced on the antiquities market in 2003. Most experts judge it a forgery.
b: The so-called Jehoash Inscription, a black stone with sixteen lines in old Hebrew script, claims to be Joash's own record of these repairs. It appeared without a known findspot. A committee of the Israel Antiquities Authority judged it a modern forgery in 2003, citing errors of language and a fake surface coating. In 2012 a long trial ended without a conviction for forgery, but the court did not rule the tablet genuine, and most epigraphers still reject it. It shows why finds without an excavation record need care.

a: Silver basins, snuffers, bowls, trumpets
p: Kings says no new vessels were made from this money. Chronicles says the surplus did make vessels.
b: Kings stresses that the money went only to the building work. 2 Chronicles 24:14 adds that when the work was done, the rest of the money was used to make vessels for the house, of gold and silver. Harmonizers say both are true in sequence: no vessels during the repairs, some afterward. Critical scholars see Chronicles' interest in the temple's worship shaping its retelling. Either way, both accounts praise the workers' honesty (12:15).

a: for they worked faithfully
p: The same words are used of Josiah's workmen two centuries later (22:7).
b: "They did not settle accounts with them, because they acted faithfully" (be'emunah) is repeated in the account of Josiah's repairs (22:7). In both, the king trusts the craftsmen and the overseers, and the narrator holds up their honesty as a model. The word 'emunah is the faithfulness by which, Habakkuk says, the righteous person lives (Habakkuk 2:4).
orig: כִּי בֶאֱמֻנָה הֵם עֹשִׂים (ki ve'emunah hem 'osim)

a: Money for guilt offerings and money for sin offerings
p: Money paid with guilt and sin offerings stayed with the priests, as their income.
b: The law allows a guilt offering to include a payment in silver and an added fifth to the priest (Leviticus 5:15–16; Numbers 5:8). The sin offering (or "purification offering," as many scholars render chatta't) was partly eaten by the priests (Leviticus 6:26). Joash's reform did not take this income away from them; it only separated the building fund from their livelihood.
orig: כֶּסֶף אָשָׁם וְכֶסֶף חַטָּאוֹת (kesef 'asham vekhesef chatta'ot)

a: made war on Gath and took it
p: Excavations at Tell es-Safi, ancient Gath, have found a siege trench and a great destruction from about 830 BC.
b: Gath, the Philistine city of Goliath, is identified with Tell es-Safi. Excavations led by Aren Maeir have uncovered a siege trench more than two kilometers long around the city and a violent destruction layer from the late ninth century BC. Most scholars connect them with Hazael's campaign. After it, Gath never recovered its earlier size, and later prophets list the Philistine cities without it (Amos 1:6–8; Zephaniah 2:4). From Gath, Jerusalem lay a day or two away.

a: He sent it all to Hazael king of Aram
p: Joash empties the treasury to save Jerusalem. Kings gives no verdict; Chronicles calls the war a judgment.
b: Kings repeatedly tells of treasuries emptied: by Shishak (1 Kings 14:26), by Asa to hire Ben-hadad (1 Kings 15:18), by Jehoash of Israel (14:14), by Ahaz (16:8) and by Hezekiah (18:15–16). Each time the temple's wealth flows out to foreign kings. Chronicles tells instead that a small Aramean army defeated Judah's large one, because Judah had abandoned the LORD, and that Joash was left badly wounded (2 Chronicles 24:23–25).

a: struck Joash down at Beth-millo
p: Kings gives no reason. Chronicles says his servants killed him to avenge the blood of Jehoiada's son.
b: Beth-millo ("house of the fill") was probably part of the terraced fill (the Millo) between the City of David and the temple mount (1 Kings 9:15). Kings reports the murder without explanation. Chronicles links it to the stoning of Zechariah son of Jehoiada and says Joash was not buried in the tombs of the kings (2 Chronicles 24:25). It also names the murderers' mothers as an Ammonite and a Moabite (2 Chronicles 24:26; see the variant at 2 Kings 12:21). Some historians suggest that the humiliating payment to Hazael cost him the support of his court.

a: In the twenty-third year of Joash
t: Synchronisms that do not add up
p: Jehoahaz begins in Joash's 23rd year and reigns 17 years, yet his son begins in Joash's 37th, not his 40th.
b: 23 plus 17 gives 40, but 13:10 dates Jehoash of Israel's accession to Joash's 37th year. Thiele solved this with a co-regency of Jehoahaz and his son, and with Israel's change of counting method. Tadmor and Cogan suspect a scribal error in one of the figures; Albright's system also had to adjust a number. Codex Vaticanus has the same figures as the Hebrew throughout chapters 13–17. The Lucianic Greek has a different system of synchronisms in the Omride chapters (Shenkel), which shows that ancient readers struggled with them too; whether it differs in these chapters could not be checked here. See the topic "Dating the Kings."

a: Jehoahaz pleaded with the LORD, and the LORD heard him
p: Sin, oppression, a cry, a deliverer: the pattern is exactly the one the book of Judges uses.
b: Judges tells Israel's history as a cycle: Israel does evil, the LORD's anger burns and he hands them to an enemy, they cry out, and he raises up a deliverer (Judges 2:11–19; Judges 3:7–9). 13:3–5 use the same words: "the LORD's anger blazed," "he gave them into the hand of," "a deliverer" (moshia', Judges 3:9, 3:15). The surprise is that it is the evil king Jehoahaz who pleads, and that the LORD listens. As in Judges, the rescue does not lead to lasting change (13:6).

a: someone to save them
p: The text does not name him. Candidates include an Assyrian king, Jehoash, Jeroboam II, and Elisha.
b: Several answers have been given. (1) Adad-nirari III of Assyria, who attacked Damascus about 796 BC and took heavy tribute from it, giving Israel breathing room; his inscriptions record this. (2) Jehoash, who won back towns from Aram (13:25). (3) Jeroboam II, through whom the LORD "rescued" Israel (14:27, the same root). (4) Elisha, whose last prophecy promised victory (13:17). Jewish commentators such as Radak named an Israelite king. Many modern historians favor Adad-nirari, though Kings would be unusual in calling an Assyrian a savior.

a: the Asherah pole still stood in Samaria
t: "The LORD of Samaria and his Asherah"
p: An inscription from about 800 BC blesses travelers "by the LORD of Samaria and his asherah."
b: At Kuntillet 'Ajrud in the Sinai, travelers about 800 BC wrote blessings on storage jars: "I bless you by YHWH of Samaria and his asherah." Scholars debate whether "his asherah" means a goddess paired with the LORD or a wooden cult object. Either way, it shows that some Israelites in exactly this period worshiped the LORD together with an Asherah, as Kings says. Ahab had set up the Asherah pole in Samaria (1 Kings 16:33); Jehu's purge of Baal did not touch it.

a: made them like dust to be trampled
p: Aram had reduced Israel's army to fifty horsemen and ten chariots. Ahab had fielded two thousand chariots at Qarqar.
b: At the battle of Qarqar in 853 BC, Shalmaneser III's inscription credits "Ahab the Israelite" with 2,000 chariots and 10,000 foot soldiers. Fifty years later Israel has ten chariots. "Like dust at threshing" echoes Amos's charge against Damascus: "they threshed Gilead with sledges of iron" (Amos 1:3). The "For" at the start of the verse links back to 13:4: this was the misery the LORD saw.

a: Jehoash son of Jehoahaz became king over Israel
p: A stela of Adad-nirari III found at Tell al-Rimah lists tribute from "Joash of Samaria."
b: The Tell al-Rimah stela, found in northern Iraq in 1967, records that Adad-nirari III received tribute from "Iu'asu (Joash) of Samaria," probably in 796 BC, the same campaign in which he humbled Damascus. Assyrian scribes otherwise usually called Israel "the house of Omri." Jehoash's tribute and Aram's weakness help explain his victories over Ben-hadad (13:25) and over Amaziah of Judah (14:8–14).

a: Israel's chariots and its riders
p: Elisha cried these words when Elijah was taken up (2:12). Now a king says them over Elisha.
b: When Elijah went up in the whirlwind, Elisha cried out, "My father! My father! Israel's chariots and riders!" (2:12). The words mean that the prophet, not the army, was Israel's true defense. Now the grandson of Jehu, whose army has been ground to dust (13:7), says the same over the dying Elisha. Elisha's ministry began and ends with the cry, and with an image of fiery chariots that once surrounded him (6:17).

a: An arrow of the LORD's saving help
p: Elisha's arrow is a prophetic sign that brings about what it shows. Shooting toward the east aims at Aram.
b: Prophets often acted out their messages: Ahijah tore a cloak into twelve pieces (1 Kings 11:30), Zedekiah son of Chenaanah made iron horns (1 Kings 22:11), and Jeremiah and Ezekiel performed many such acts (Jeremiah 19:10; Ezekiel 4–5). Shooting an arrow toward an enemy's land is also known from ancient rites declaring war, and Ezekiel describes the king of Babylon divining with arrows (Ezekiel 21:21). Elisha's hands on the king's hands show that the victory is the LORD's (teshu'ah, "saving help"), and Aphek recalls Ahab's victory over Aram there (1 Kings 20:26–30).

a: Five or six beats, that is what it needed!
p: The king was not told how many times to strike. Elisha's anger suggests the king lacked eagerness, or faith.
b: Some readers find the scene unfair: the king did what he was told. Most interpreters answer that a sign-act calls for the doer's full engagement, and that striking only three times showed a half-hearted king who did not expect much from God. Others see a test of zeal, like Gideon's men at the water (Judges 7:5–7). The result is precise: Jehoash defeats Aram three times (13:25), enough to win back towns but not to finish Aram.

a: as each year came in
t: "At the coming in of the year"
p: Raiders came each spring, when the harvest was ripe and armies took the field.
b: The Hebrew ba shanah, literally "a year came," is odd; with a small change it reads "at the coming of the year," that is, in spring (compare 2 Samuel 11:1, "When the year came around again, at the season when kings march out"). Moab had broken free from Israel under Mesha (3:4–5), and its raiding bands now crossed the Jordan into Israel's land.

a: when he touched Elisha's bones he came to life
p: Even dead, Elisha gives life. Jews, Christians and skeptics have read the scene in very different ways.
b: Ben Sira praised Elisha because even in death his body prophesied and his works were wonders (Sirach 48:13–14). The Talmud asks who the man was and teaches that he stood up only so as not to stay buried beside a righteous man, and did not live long (Bavli Sanhedrin 47a). Christian writers such as Cyril of Jerusalem used the story to defend honoring the relics of saints and as a sign of the resurrection (Catechetical Lectures 18.16). Matthew's tombs opening at Jesus' death (Matthew 27:52) have been compared. Critical scholars see a prophetic legend that shows Elisha's power outliving him.

a: his covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
p: This is the only time Kings grounds God's mercy on the covenant with the three patriarchs.
b: Elsewhere Kings speaks of God's promise to David or of the covenant at Horeb. Here, uniquely, the LORD spares Israel "for the sake of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob," as when he "remembered his covenant" in Egypt (Exodus 2:24) and as Leviticus promises even after exile (Leviticus 26:42). "Until now" may show that this sentence was written while the northern kingdom still stood, or that the writer means God's patience lasted until the end told in chapter 17.

a: his son Ben-hadad became king
p: The Zakkur inscription from Hamath names "Bar-hadad son of Hazael" as leader of a coalition.
b: The Zakkur stela (about 800 BC) describes how "Bar-hadad son of Hazael, king of Aram," led a coalition of kings to besiege Zakkur in Hazrach, and how Baalshamayn delivered him. Ben-hadad is the Hebrew form of the same name. His failure there, together with Assyria's pressure, fits Aram's weakening in 13:25. This is a different Ben-hadad from Ahab's opponent (1 Kings 20).

a: Three times Joash struck him down
p: Exactly as Elisha said: three strikes on the ground, three victories over Aram (13:19).
b: The narrator closes the chapter by showing Elisha's sign fulfilled to the letter (13:18–19). The towns Jehoash won back were probably west of the Jordan, lost under his father (13:3, 13:7); the lands east of the Jordan were recovered only under Jeroboam II (14:25, 14:28).

a: as it is written in the book of the law of Moses
p: Amaziah spares the killers' sons because the law forbids punishing children for their fathers' crimes.
b: The quotation matches Deuteronomy 24:16 almost exactly: "Fathers must not be put to death because of their children, and children must not be put to death because of their fathers. Each one is to be put to death for his own sin" (Deuteronomy 24:16). It is one of the very few places where Kings quotes the written law, and it sets Amaziah apart from the custom of wiping out a rival's family (9:26; 10:6–11; 11:1). Some ancient law codes did punish children for their parents' crimes (Hammurabi's laws 229–230). The principle is developed by Jeremiah and Ezekiel (Jeremiah 31:29–30; Ezekiel 18:20). Critical scholars see the hand of a Deuteronomistic editor.

a: He seized Sela in battle
p: Sela means "Rock." It was once identified with Petra; most scholars now look for it near Bozrah in northern Edom.
b: Ha-sela', "the Rock," was long equated with Petra, the later Nabatean city, partly because the Greek name Petra also means rock. Excavations show no major Iron Age town at Petra's center, and many scholars now identify Sela with es-Sela', a rock fortress near Bozrah. Chronicles adds a harsh detail, that ten thousand captives were thrown down from "the top of the rock" (2 Chronicles 25:11–12), and that Amaziah "brought the gods of the people of Seir with him and stood them up to be his gods. He bowed down before them" (2 Chronicles 25:14). The Valley of Salt, south of the Dead Sea, was also the site of David's victory over Edom (2 Samuel 8:13).

a: let us look each other in the face
p: "Let us see each other's faces" sounds friendly but is a challenge to fight. 14:11 shows what it meant.
b: The reflexive verb nitra'eh fanim, "let us look at each other face to face," is a polite-sounding way to say "let us meet in battle," as 14:11 makes clear. Chronicles supplies a motive: Amaziah had hired a hundred thousand Israelite soldiers, then sent them home at a prophet's word, and they raided Judah's towns on the way (2 Chronicles 25:6–13). Kings suggests instead that his victory over Edom had gone to his head (14:10).

a: The thornbush in Lebanon
p: Jehoash answers with a fable, like Jotham's in Judges 9: a lowly thornbush aspires above its station.
b: Fables in which trees and plants talk are rare in the Bible. The other is Jotham's, where the thornbush says, "If not, may fire go out from the thornbush and devour the cedars of Lebanon!" (Judges 9:15). Here the thornbush (Amaziah) asks the mighty cedar (Jehoash) for a marriage between equals, and a passing wild animal crushes it. The point is mockery: Amaziah is not the cedar's equal and should stay home. Similar plant disputes are known from Mesopotamian literature.

a: four hundred cubits
p: About 600 feet (180 meters) of the north wall was torn down, from the Gate of Ephraim to the Corner Gate.
b: A cubit was about 18 inches (45 centimeters), so the breach was about 600 feet long. The Gate of Ephraim faced north toward Ephraim, and the Corner Gate probably stood at the northwest corner of the city of that time (Jeremiah 31:38; Zechariah 14:10). The north was Jerusalem's weak side, where the ground is level. Uzziah later built towers at the Corner Gate and fortified the walls (2 Chronicles 26:9), perhaps to repair this very damage.

a: people given as pledges
p: "Sons of pledges" means hostages, held to guarantee that Judah would keep the peace.
b: Bene hatta'arubot, "sons of the pledges," occurs only here and in the parallel (2 Chronicles 25:24). Taking members of noble or royal families as hostages was common practice in the ancient Near East; Assyria and Egypt both did it. Together with the breach in the wall and the plundered treasury, it shows that Judah became, for a time, a dependent of Israel.

a: he ran to Lachish
p: Lachish was Judah's second city, a great fortress in the lowland southwest of Jerusalem.
b: Lachish (Tel Lachish) guarded the road from the coast into the hills. Its massive walls are best known from Sennacherib's siege in 701 BC (18:14; 19:8), pictured on reliefs from Nineveh. Amaziah fled there because it was the strongest place in Judah outside Jerusalem. Chronicles dates the plot "from the time Amaziah turned away from following the LORD" (2 Chronicles 25:27).

a: Azariah
p: This king is called Azariah in 14:21–15:7 and Uzziah in 15:13–34, as in Isaiah, Amos and Chronicles.
b: Both names honor the LORD: 'Azaryah, "the LORD has helped," and 'Uzziyyah, "my strength is the LORD." The two roots are close in meaning, and some scholars think one was a throne name and the other a personal name. The prophets know him as Uzziah (Isaiah 1:1; Isaiah 6:1; Amos 1:1; Hosea 1:1), as does Chronicles (2 Chronicles 26:1), while 1 Chronicles 3:12 has Azariah. An "Azriyau" in the annals of Tiglath-pileser III was once thought to be this king; most scholars now see him as a ruler in northern Syria.

a: built up Elath
p: Elath, at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, gave Judah a port for trade with Arabia, as in Solomon's day.
b: Elath (or Eloth) lay near Ezion-geber, where Solomon built ships (1 Kings 9:26) and Jehoshaphat's fleet was wrecked (1 Kings 22:48). Judah lost Edom under Jehoram (8:20–22). Rebuilding Elath meant control of the road through Edom and the trade of the Red Sea. It was lost again under Ahaz (16:6). "After the king had lain down" seems to date the work after Amaziah's death, though some read it as Azariah's work while his father was still alive.

a: Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel, became king
p: The second Jeroboam ruled Israel's richest age. Amos and Hosea preached in his reign.
b: Jeroboam II reigned forty-one years, about 793–753 BC in Thiele's system, which counts a co-regency with his father from 793. Others date his sole reign to about 788 or 786–746 (Albright). Aram and Assyria were both weak, and Israel grew rich. The Samaria ostraca, records of wine and oil deliveries found in the capital, probably come from his time. The prophets Amos and Hosea saw the other side: ivory beds, great houses and the poor sold for a pair of sandals (Amos 2:6; Amos 6:4–7). Kings gives his long reign only seven verses.

a: Jonah son of Amittai
p: This is the same Jonah whom God later sends to Nineveh, in the book that bears his name.
b: "The word of the LORD came to Jonah son of Amittai" (Jonah 1:1) opens the book of Jonah. Here the same prophet gives a word of hope to Israel under a king who did evil. Gath-hepher was a town in Zebulun in Galilee (Joshua 19:13), and a traditional tomb of Jonah is shown at nearby Mashhad. Jesus, a Galilean himself, pointed to "the sign of Jonah" (Matthew 12:39–41). Jewish tradition identified Jonah with the widow's son whom Elijah raised and with the young prophet of 9:4 (see the note there). The book's sharp turn, from a patriot prophet to a messenger of mercy to Assyria, has long been noticed.

a: from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah
p: Jeroboam regains Israel's ideal northern and southern limits. Amos uses the same two points to announce the opposite.
b: Lebo-hamath, "the entrance of Hamath," in the Beqaa valley of Lebanon, was the ideal northern border (Numbers 34:8; 1 Kings 8:65). The Sea of the Arabah is the Dead Sea (Deuteronomy 3:17). Amos, preaching in Jeroboam's reign, threatens a nation that will oppress Israel "from Lebo-hamath to the wadi of the Arabah" (Amos 6:14). The prophecies of Jonah and Amos stand side by side: one promised the borders back, the other warned that they would be lost.

a: There was no one, bound or free
t: An echo of the Song of Moses
p: The phrase comes from Deuteronomy 32:36, where God has pity when his people's strength is gone.
b: The Song of Moses says the LORD will show his servants pity "when he sees their strength has run out and no one is left, whether held fast or set loose" (Deuteronomy 32:36). Kings borrows the same pair of words ('atsur and 'azuv) used in the dynastic curses (9:8), and the Plain renders them the same way, "bound" and "free", but here they describe Israel's helplessness, not its punishment. "Very bitter" translates moreh, probably from marar, "be bitter"; the gloss "rebellious" sometimes given for it does not fit.

a: The LORD had never spoken of erasing Israel's name from under the sky
p: Deuteronomy warns of a name wiped out "from under the sky." For now, the LORD has not said that about Israel.
b: The words recall Moses' plea after the golden calf, when the LORD said, "Let go of me, so I can destroy them and wipe out their name from under the sky" (Deuteronomy 9:14), and the curse on the idolater (Deuteronomy 29:20). Kings stresses that the LORD saves even under an evil king, out of pity. The word "not" hangs over the next three chapters: about thirty years after Jeroboam's death, Samaria falls (17:6, 17:18).

a: how he brought Damascus and Hamath back to Judah in Israel
p: The Hebrew says "he returned Damascus and Hamath to Judah in Israel." Its meaning is disputed.
b: Literally: "he brought back Damascus and Hamath to Judah in Israel." Readings include: (1) he recovered for Israel lands that had belonged to Judah, that is, to David and Solomon's united kingdom (2 Samuel 8:5–10; 1 Kings 11:24); (2) "Judah" is a copying slip, and the original said only "to Israel"; (3) "to Judah" should be read "to Yaudi," a Syrian state, or the phrase means he made these places Israel's vassals. The Plain keeps the literal words and leaves the sense open. Damascus itself was probably never ruled by Jeroboam, though Aram was weak enough then to pay him tribute.
orig: הֵשִׁיב אֶת־דַּמֶּשֶׂק וְאֶת־חֲמָת לִיהוּדָה בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל (heshiv 'et-dammeseq ve'et-chamat lihudah beyisra'el)

a: In the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam
p: If Amaziah outlived Jehoash by fifteen years, Azariah should start in Jeroboam's fifteenth year, not his twenty-seventh.
b: 14:17 and 14:23 put Jeroboam's accession in Amaziah's fifteenth year and Amaziah's death fifteen years after Jehoash's, which leaves the 27 years here hard to fit. Thiele explained it with overlapping reigns: Azariah ruled as co-regent from 792, when his father was captured (14:13), and Jeroboam as co-regent with his father from 793. Galil's system also uses co-regencies here. Tadmor, Cogan and Hayes–Hooker allow for error or for different starting points in the sources. The figure "fifty-two years" (15:2) likely includes the years Azariah shared the throne.

a: he had a skin disease
p: Tsara'at is a range of skin diseases, not Hansen's disease. Chronicles explains why the king was struck.
b: Older translations say "leper," but the biblical tsara'at covers many visible skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean (Leviticus 13). Kings gives no reason for the affliction. Chronicles says Uzziah grew proud, entered the temple to burn incense, a task for the priests alone, and that skin disease broke out on his forehead while the priests watched (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Josephus adds that an earthquake split the temple at that moment (Antiquities 9.10.4), linking it to the earthquake of Amos 1:1 and Zechariah 14:5.

a: He lived in a house set apart
p: Bet hachofshit means "house of freedom": release from royal duties, or a polite word for isolation.
b: Chofshi means free, as of a released slave (Exodus 21:2). The phrase may mean a house where the king was "released" from his duties, or a separate dwelling (as the Targum and many commentators take it). In the Ugaritic Baal myths, Mot's underworld is called by a similar phrase, "house of freedom," and some scholars suggest a dark euphemism, "house of the dead man," for someone cut off from life. The law required a person with skin disease to live outside the camp (Leviticus 13:46).

a: Jotham, the king's son, was over the house
p: Jotham ran the government while his father lived in isolation. This is the clearest co-regency in Kings.
b: "Over the house" is the title of the palace administrator (1 Kings 4:6; 18:18). Jotham held it and also "judged the people of the land," the work of a king. This explicit sharing of rule is the main support for the co-regency theories used to make the reign figures fit (see 15:1 and 15:32–33). An Aramaic plaque from the first century AD, now in the Israel Museum, reads: "Here were brought the bones of Uzziah king of Judah. Do not open." His remains were apparently reburied in the Second Temple period.

a: So came true the word the LORD had spoken to Jehu
p: Zechariah, fourth after Jehu, lasts six months. The promise of 10:30 is kept, and Hosea's warning too.
b: The narrator counts carefully: Jehoahaz, Jehoash, Jeroboam and Zechariah are the four generations promised in 10:30. Hosea, who prophesied that God would "bring the blood shed at Jezreel down on the house of Jehu" (Hosea 1:4), saw the dynasty end in a palace murder. With it, the northern kingdom enters its last thirty years: six kings, four of them assassinated (15:10, 15:14, 15:25, 15:30).

a: he cut open all its women who were pregnant
p: Ripping open pregnant women was an atrocity of ancient warfare, condemned by the prophets.
b: Elisha had wept because Hazael would do this to Israel (8:12). Amos condemns the Ammonites for it (Amos 1:13), and Hosea foresees it for Samaria (Hosea 13:16). An Assyrian hymn praises Tiglath-pileser I for slitting the wombs of pregnant women, so it was boasted of as well as condemned. Kings records that an Israelite king did it to an Israelite town that refused him. Where Tiphsah was is unknown: the name is that of a city on the Euphrates (1 Kings 4:24), far out of reach, and many scholars prefer the Greek reading "Tappuah" (see the variant).

a: Pul king of Assyria
p: Babylonian records call Tiglath-pileser III "Pulu." His own annals list Menahem of Samaria among the kings who paid him.
b: Tiglath-pileser III (745–727 BC) ruled Babylon under the name Pulu, as Babylonian King List A shows; Ptolemy's later king list calls him Poros. 1 Chronicles 5:26 mentions "Pul king of Assyria and Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria," which may mean "Pul, that is, Tiglath-pileser." His annals and a stela found in western Iran list "Menahem of Samaria" (Menihimme Samerinaya) among the kings who paid tribute, about 738 BC (some date it 740). Here Kings and Assyria tell the same story.

a: fifty shekels of silver for each man
p: A thousand talents at fifty shekels a head means about sixty thousand men of means paid the tax.
b: A talent was three thousand shekels, so a thousand talents was three million shekels, or about 37 tons (34 metric tons) of silver at about 11 grams to the shekel. At fifty shekels each, sixty thousand men paid. The figure shows how many free landholders the kingdom still had, and how heavy Assyrian protection was. Menahem's tax probably bred the anti-Assyrian anger that brought Pekah to power two years after his death.

a: with Argob and with Arieh
p: Argob and Arieh may be two of Pekahiah's officers who died with him, or place names misplaced from 15:29.
b: Argob is elsewhere a region of Bashan (Deuteronomy 3:4), and Arieh means "the lion." Some scholars think the words were once part of the list of places taken by Tiglath-pileser (15:29) and slipped into this verse; others take them as royal guards or princes who were killed with the king. The fifty Gileadites show that Pekah's base was east of the Jordan, which matters for the chronology of his reign (see 15:27).

a: for twenty years
p: Pekah cannot have reigned twenty years after Pekahiah: Menahem paid Assyria about 738, and Pekah died by 732.
b: This is the hardest puzzle in the chronology of the kings. Solutions: (1) Thiele: Pekah ruled a rival kingdom in Gilead from 752, when Menahem took Samaria, and became sole king in 740; Hosea's "Israel and Ephraim" (Hosea 5:5) is taken as a hint of two kingdoms. (2) Pekah later counted his reign from Menahem's accession, to deny that Menahem's house had ever been legitimate. (3) The figure is a scribal error or an inflation; Tadmor, Cogan and Albright give Pekah only about five years (Albright 737–732, Tadmor and Cogan about 735–732). Galil and Hayes–Hooker each fit the figures in their own ways. No solution has won general agreement.

a: Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came and took
p: Assyrian inscriptions describe the same campaign. Hazor and other northern towns show burned layers from this time.
b: Tiglath-pileser's campaigns of 734–732 BC took Galilee, the coast and Gilead from Israel and turned them into Assyrian provinces. Fragments of his inscriptions name towns of "the house of Omri" and boast of deporting their people to Assyria. The excavations at Hazor found a thick destruction layer from these years. Isaiah looks ahead from this dark moment: "Galilee of the nations" will see a great light (Isaiah 9:1–2), words Matthew applies to Jesus' ministry in Galilee (Matthew 4:13–16).

a: in the twentieth year of Jotham son of Uzziah
p: Tiglath-pileser claims that the Israelites overthrew Pekah and that he himself made Hoshea king.
b: An inscription of Tiglath-pileser says: "They overthrew Pekah their king, and I set Hoshea as king over them," and records the tribute he then received. Kings tells it as a plot by Hoshea; both may be true if Hoshea acted with Assyria's backing. The date is a puzzle: Jotham reigned sixteen years (15:33), so his "twentieth year" must count from the start of his reign without stopping at its end, or reflect a co-regency with Ahaz. 17:1 dates the same event to Ahaz's twelfth year, which does not fit either; Thiele himself thought a later editor had miscalculated there.

a: It was he who built the upper gate of the LORD's house
p: Chronicles adds more of Jotham's work: walls on the Ophel, towns and forts in Judah's hills, and a victory over Ammon.
b: The upper gate may be the same as the "upper gate of Benjamin" where Jeremiah was put in the stocks (Jeremiah 20:2) or the north gate of Ezekiel's vision (Ezekiel 9:2). Chronicles credits Jotham with building on the wall of the Ophel and with towns, forts and towers, and says the Ammonites paid him tribute (2 Chronicles 27:3–5). It explains his strength by his faithfulness (2 Chronicles 27:6).

a: the LORD started sending Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah into Judah
p: Damascus and Israel tried to force Judah into a revolt against Assyria. The crisis is the setting of Isaiah 7.
b: Rezin of Damascus and Pekah of Israel formed an alliance against Assyria and wanted Judah to join. When Judah refused, they attacked, aiming to put their own man, "the son of Tabeel," on David's throne (Isaiah 7:6). Historians call this the Syro-Ephraimite war (about 735–732 BC). Kings says the LORD "started sending" them, so that the attack is God's doing, and it began already under Jotham. The story continues in 16:5–9.

a: Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king
p: Ahaz is twenty at accession and reigns sixteen years; his son Hezekiah is twenty-five at his own accession (18:2).
b: Taken at face value, Ahaz would have been about eleven when Hezekiah was born. Solutions include: a co-regency of Ahaz with Jotham, so that his sixteen years started earlier than his sole rule; an error in one of the ages (some Greek and Syriac copies of 2 Chronicles 28:1 make Ahaz twenty-five); or a different date for Hezekiah's accession (729 or 715 BC, a famous debate tied to 18:1, 18:9–10 and 18:13). Thiele dates Ahaz about 735–715 BC.

a: He even made his son pass through the fire
t: Child sacrifice or a fire rite?
p: Most scholars think Ahaz burned his son as a sacrifice. Some Jewish interpreters read a rite of passing between fires.
b: Deuteronomy forbids "anyone who makes his son or his daughter pass through the fire" (Deuteronomy 18:10) and says the nations "even burn their sons and their daughters in the fire for their gods" (Deuteronomy 12:31). Chronicles says Ahaz "burned his sons in the fire" in the Valley of Ben-hinnom (2 Chronicles 28:3). Most scholars therefore take the phrase as child sacrifice, which Jeremiah describes at the Topheth (Jeremiah 7:31). The rabbis read it as a rite of dedication in which the child passed between fires without being killed (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:7; Bavli Sanhedrin 64b; Rashi on Leviticus 18:21), a view some modern scholars share. Kings does not say which son. A rabbinic tradition holds that it was Hezekiah, who survived (Bavli Sanhedrin 63b).

a: They hemmed Ahaz in, but they were not able to win the fight
t: Isaiah 7 and the sign of Immanuel
p: Isaiah 7:1 repeats this sentence almost word for word, then tells how the prophet met Ahaz and gave him a sign.
b: Isaiah 7 begins with nearly the same words, then tells that when the house of David heard that Aram had allied with Ephraim, Ahaz's heart shook the way forest trees shake in a wind (Isaiah 7:2). Isaiah urged him to trust God, not Assyria, with a play on words: "If you will not hold firm, you will not be held firm" (Isaiah 7:9). When Ahaz refused to ask for a sign, God gave one: a young woman would bear a son named Immanuel (Isaiah 7:14). Matthew reads that sign as fulfilled in Jesus' birth (Matthew 1:22–23). Kings tells none of this, only that Ahaz chose Assyria (16:7).

a: came up to Jerusalem for battle
p: Chronicles tells of huge defeats, and of captives sent home kindly. Some see the seed of a famous parable.
b: Kings says only that the attackers could not take Jerusalem. Chronicles says Aram took many captives to Damascus, and Israel killed 120,000 Judeans in a day and took 200,000 captives (2 Chronicles 28:5–8). Then the prophet Oded rebuked Israel, and men of Ephraim clothed the captives, gave them food, drink and oil, put the weak on donkeys and brought them to Jericho (2 Chronicles 28:9–15). Many readers have noticed how closely this resembles Jesus' parable of the Samaritan who helped a man on the Jericho road (Luke 10:30–35).

a: the Judeans
p: Yehudim, "Judeans," appears here for the first time in the Bible. It is the word that later becomes "Jews."
b: Yehudi first means a person of the kingdom of Judah. After the exile, when Judah was the only part of Israel left as a recognizable people, it came to mean any Israelite, and so "Jew" (Esther 2:5, "a Jewish man whose name was Mordecai ... a man of Benjamin"). The KJV renders it "the Jews" here. The Plain uses "Judeans" because the setting is the kingdom of Judah, and because "Jews" would suggest a religious identity that came later.

a: I am your servant and your son
p: "Servant" and "son" are treaty words. Tiglath-pileser lists "Jehoahaz of Judah" among his tributaries.
b: In treaty language a vassal is his lord's "servant" and "son" (compare 2 Samuel 10:19). Ahaz offers both, putting the words first in Hebrew ("Your servant and your son am I"), and adds the bribe of 16:8. An inscription of Tiglath-pileser lists "Jehoahaz (Iauhazi) of Judah" among the kings who paid him tribute about 734 BC: Ahaz is a shortened form of Jehoahaz, with God's name left off. Isaiah had urged the opposite course, to trust in the LORD rather than in Assyria (Isaiah 7:4–9). Chronicles says Assyria's king "pressed him hard and did not strengthen him" (2 Chronicles 28:20). The word "servant" ('eved) can mean slave, servant or vassal; here it is political.

a: he sent the king of Assyria a bribe
p: Shochad is the Law's word for a bribe that corrupts justice. Kings chooses it on purpose.
b: A payment to a foreign king could be called a gift or tribute (minchah, 17:3). Kings uses shochad, the word the Law forbids judges to take because "a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise" (Deuteronomy 16:19; Exodus 23:8). Asa's payment to Ben-hadad was called the same (1 Kings 15:19). The choice of word passes judgment: Ahaz bought help with the LORD's treasures. An unprovenanced seal impression reading "Belonging to Ahaz son of Jotham, king of Judah" was published in the 1990s; its age is debated.

a: took its people away captive to Kir
p: Amos had foretold that Aram's people would go into exile to Kir, the land the Arameans came from.
