b: Amos 1:5 says the people of Aram "will go into exile to Kir," and Amos 9:7 says God brought the Arameans up from Kir, as he brought Israel from Egypt. Damascus fell to Tiglath-pileser in 732 BC, and his annals record Rezin's defeat. With Damascus gone, nothing stood between Assyria and Samaria. Kir's location is unknown; some place it in Mesopotamia near Elam (Isaiah 22:6).

a: the altar that stood in Damascus
t: Why did Ahaz copy the altar?
p: Older scholars thought Assyria forced its religion on vassals. Most now think Ahaz chose an Aramean-style altar himself.
b: One view holds that the altar was Assyrian and that copying it was a sign of political submission required by Tiglath-pileser. Studies by Mordechai Cogan and John McKay argued that Assyria did not generally impose its gods on vassal states such as Judah, and that the altar was probably Aramean or simply fashionable, a large altar for burnt offerings in the style of the region. On that reading Ahaz chose to imitate his new world, and Kings condemns the change because it moved the LORD's bronze altar aside. Uriah the priest is probably the trustworthy witness Isaiah named (Isaiah 8:2).

a: that will be for me to inquire by
t: What did Ahaz want the bronze altar for?
p: Levaqqer may mean "to inquire," perhaps by reading a sacrifice's organs, or "to consider" later.
b: The verb biqqer means "to look closely, to examine" (Leviticus 13:36; Leviticus 27:33). Many scholars think Ahaz kept the old altar for divination, perhaps by inspecting the livers of sacrificed animals, an art highly developed in Mesopotamia (Ezekiel 21:21 mentions it). Others, including several Jewish commentators, take it as "it will be for me to think about," that is, Ahaz will decide its use later. Either way, the LORD's altar loses its central place.

a: He lowered the Sea from the bronze oxen
p: Ahaz strips Solomon's bronze stands and takes the great basin off its twelve bronze oxen.
b: Solomon's bronze Sea stood on twelve bronze oxen, and ten wheeled stands each held a basin (1 Kings 7:23–39). Ahaz removes the decorated panels and the oxen, perhaps to send their bronze to Assyria as tribute, perhaps to remove images that offended his new overlord, or simply to change the courtyard. The Babylonians would later break up what was left and carry off the bronze (25:13–16).

a: The Sabbath covering
p: Neither the "covered structure for the Sabbath" nor the king's outer entrance is known from elsewhere.
b: The Ketiv and Qere spell the first word differently (misakh / musakh), and its meaning is guessed from the root "to cover": a canopy, a covered walkway or a royal stand used on the Sabbath. The "king's outer entrance" was the king's private way into the temple. Ahaz altered or removed both "because of the king of Assyria," perhaps to strip signs of royal independence, perhaps for fear of him. The Greek translators had trouble with the words too.

a: In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah
t: A date that does not fit
p: 15:30 dates Hoshea's accession by Jotham, this verse by Ahaz's twelfth year. The two cannot both fit.
b: Hoshea took the throne about 732/731 BC, when Tiglath-pileser confirmed him. If Ahaz began in 735 (Thiele), his twelfth year would be about 723, not 732. Thiele concluded that the synchronisms of 17:1 and 18:1, 18:9–10 were calculated by a later editor who did not know of the overlaps, and so are twelve years off. Others think Ahaz's reign is counted from an earlier co-regency, or that one figure is corrupt. See the topic "Dating the Kings."

a: only not like the kings of Israel who were before him
p: Kings does not say. Jewish tradition says Hoshea removed the guards that kept Israelites from going to Jerusalem.
b: The last king of Israel is judged more gently than the rest, but the kingdom falls in his time. The Talmud lists among the joys of the fifteenth of Av "the day Hoshea son of Elah removed the guards that Jeroboam had placed on the roads" to stop pilgrims from going to Jerusalem (Bavli Taanit 30b–31a; Bavli Bava Batra 121b). Some modern scholars suggest the calves had already been taken by Assyria (Hosea 10:5–6). Either way, the end is not the punishment of one king but of centuries (17:7–23).

a: Shalmaneser king of Assyria
p: Shalmaneser V ruled Assyria 727–722 BC. A Babylonian chronicle says he "ravaged Samaria."
b: Tiglath-pileser's son Shalmaneser V reigned only five years, and few of his own inscriptions survive. The Babylonian Chronicle records that in his reign "he ravaged Shamara'in," which most scholars read as Samaria, though a few read a town in Syria. Kings names him as the one who besieged Samaria (17:5; 18:9). Hoshea had paid tribute to Tiglath-pileser (15:30) and continued with his son, until he gambled on Egypt.

a: So king of Egypt
p: No pharaoh named So is known. Suggestions include Osorkon IV, the city of Sais, and a title.
b: Egypt was divided among rival dynasties about 725 BC. Proposals: (1) So is a short form of Osorkon IV, king at Tanis in the Delta, the nearest Egyptian ruler (Kitchen); (2) "So" is the city Sais, and the text first said "to Sais, to the king of Egypt," meaning Tefnakht, the ruler there (Goedicke); (3) he is the Nubian king Piye (Piankhy), whose dynasty was moving into Egypt (Kittel; revived by W. Shea, who points to the Lucianic Greek; see the variant). An older idea that "So" was an official's title (Yeivin) has been given up. Hosea mocks Israel's swings between powers: "Ephraim has turned into a dove: silly, no mind of its own. They have called to Egypt; they have gone off to Assyria" (Hosea 7:11). Egypt sent no help.

a: held it under siege three years
t: Hoshea's arrest and the long siege
p: Hoshea seems to be in prison before the siege begins. Samaria held out about three years without its king.
b: 17:4 says Hoshea was arrested; 17:5 then tells of the siege. Either Hoshea went out to Shalmaneser to make peace and was seized, leaving the city to fight on, or the verses summarize rather than tell events in order. Three years, counted inclusively, may be two years and some months, about 724–722 BC (18:9–10). Samaria's hilltop walls made it hard to take.

a: the king of Assyria took Samaria
t: Who took Samaria: Shalmaneser or Sargon?
p: Kings implies Shalmaneser. Sargon II, his successor, claimed the conquest and the deportation of 27,290 people.
b: Sargon II (722–705 BC) boasts: "I besieged and conquered Samaria. I carried off 27,290 of the people who lived in it. I formed a unit of fifty chariots from among them. I settled in it people from lands I had conquered" (a second copy gives 27,280). The Babylonian Chronicle credits Shalmaneser V with ravaging the city. Most historians, following Tadmor, think Shalmaneser took Samaria in 722, just before he died, and Sargon put down a revolt there in 720 and organized the deportation; others give the whole conquest to one king. Kings' "the king of Assyria" can cover both.

a: in Halah, by the Habor River of Gozan, and in the towns of Media
p: Assyrian documents with Israelite names have been found at Gozan and other sites, matching these places.
b: Halah lay northeast of Nineveh; the Habor (modern Khabur) is a tributary of the Euphrates, with Gozan (Tell Halaf) on its banks; Media lay east in the Zagros mountains, conquered by Sargon about 716 BC. Business documents from Gozan and from Dur-Katlimmu on the Khabur include people with names built on "Yahu," the LORD's name, and Assyrian lists of soldiers include a chariot unit of "Samarians." They show that some of the exiles kept Israelite names for generations. The Greek has "the mountains of the Medes" (see the variant). See the topic "The Lost Tribes of Israel."

a: It came about because the Israelites sinned against the LORD their God
p: 17:7–23 is a sermon explaining the fall of Samaria. Who wrote it, and when, is debated.
b: The passage is the longest comment by the narrator in Kings. Its language comes from Deuteronomy: other gods, high places, standing stones, Asherah poles, "stiff necks," the prophets ignored. Traditional readers see a prophetic historian, Jeremiah in Jewish tradition (Bavli Bava Batra 15a), explaining God's justice. Most critical scholars see the hand of the Deuteronomistic editors: an earlier layer about Israel, and later additions about Judah (17:13, 17:19–20) written after Jerusalem fell in 586. Either way, it reads the end of Israel not as an Assyrian success but as the covenant curses coming true (Deuteronomy 28:36, 28:64).

a: did things in secret against the LORD their God
p: Wayechappe'u occurs only here. It may mean "did secretly," "covered over," or "spoke words that were not right."
b: The root is related to chafah, "to cover" (2 Samuel 15:30). Ancient translations guessed: the Greek has "clothed themselves" with words; the Vulgate "offended the Lord with things that were not right"; the Targum "devised words." Modern versions split between "secretly did" and "did things that were not right." The point is hypocrisy: outward worship of the LORD, hidden worship of others, as the following verses make plain.

a: on every high hill and under every leafy tree
p: The phrase comes from Deuteronomy 12:2 and recurs through Kings, Jeremiah and Ezekiel.
b: Deuteronomy ordered Israel to destroy the places where the nations worshiped "on the high mountains, on the hills, and under every leafy tree" (Deuteronomy 12:2). Kings applies it to Rehoboam's Judah (1 Kings 14:23) and Ahaz (16:4), and Jeremiah uses it again and again of Judah's unfaithfulness (Jeremiah 2:20; Jeremiah 3:6, 3:13). Green trees, perhaps sacred groves, and hilltops were thought to be places where the gods were near.
r: Deuteronomy 12:2; 1 Kings 14:23; 16:4; Jeremiah 2:20; Jeremiah 3:6; Ezekiel 6:13; Hosea 4:13

a: by every prophet and every visionary
p: The LORD's warnings came through prophet after prophet, a theme taken up by Jeremiah, Zechariah and Jesus.
b: The "visionary" (chozeh) is a second word for a prophet, kept distinct from the "seer" (ro'eh). "Turn back from your evil roads" is almost the exact message the post-exilic prophet Zechariah sums up as the call of "the former prophets" (Zechariah 1:4), and Jeremiah complains that the LORD sent his servants the prophets "again and again" (Jeremiah 7:25; Jeremiah 25:4–5). The theme of rejected messengers is taken up in Nehemiah's prayer (Nehemiah 9:26, 9:30) and in Jesus' parable of the tenants (Mark 12:1–9). Mentioning Judah already here may point to an editor writing after 586.
r: Zechariah 1:4–6; Jeremiah 7:25–26; Jeremiah 25:4–5; Nehemiah 9:26; Nehemiah 9:30; Mark 12:1–9; Matthew 23:37

a: They hardened their necks
p: The picture is of an ox that will not bend its neck to the yoke. Moses used it of the wilderness generation.
b: God called Israel "a stiff-necked people" at the golden calf (Exodus 32:9), and Moses told them, "I know your defiance and your stiff neck" (Deuteronomy 31:27). Kings links the last generation of Israel to the first: "like their ancestors' necks." Stephen uses the same words against the council in Jerusalem (Acts 7:51).

a: They went after vapor and became vapor
p: Hevel, "breath, vapor," is a name for idols. Those who follow emptiness become empty.
b: Hevel is the word Ecclesiastes uses for life's fleeting breath ("vapor of vapors," Ecclesiastes 1:2), and the prophets use it for idols (Jeremiah 10:15; Deuteronomy 32:21). The wordplay wayyelkhu 'achare hahevel wayyehbalu appears word for word in Jeremiah 2:5, where God asks, "What crooked thing did your ancestors find in me, that they moved away from me and walked after vapor and became vapor?" The thought that worshipers become like what they worship is also in Psalm 115:8. Translations vary: "worthless idols," "vanity," "false gods."
orig: וַיֵּלְכוּ אַחֲרֵי הַהֶבֶל וַיֶּהְבָּלוּ (vayyelkhu 'achare hahevel vayyehbalu)

a: the whole army of the sky
p: Worship of the sun, moon and stars is forbidden in Deuteronomy. Kings blames it on Israel here and on Manasseh in 21:3.
b: Deuteronomy warns, "when you raise your eyes to the sky and see the sun, the moon and the stars, the whole army of the sky, do not be pulled away to bow down to them" (Deuteronomy 4:19). Astral worship was widespread in Mesopotamia and Syria, and Kings charges Manasseh with it (21:3, 21:5) and has Josiah remove it (23:4–5). Some scholars think the charge against the northern kingdom reflects later Judean practice read back into Israel.

a: they sold themselves to do evil in the LORD's eyes
p: "Sold himself to do evil" was said only of Ahab. Now it describes the whole nation.
b: Elijah told Ahab, "I have found you, because you sold yourself to do what the LORD sees as evil" (1 Kings 21:20), and the narrator added that there was no one like Ahab, "who sold himself to do what the LORD sees as evil" (1 Kings 21:25). The phrase now covers all Israel. The list of sins in this verse (passing children through fire, divination, omens) repeats the forbidden practices of Deuteronomy 18:10.

a: None were left except the tribe of Judah by itself
p: Only Judah remained. Archaeology suggests many northerners fled south, and Jerusalem grew several times over.
b: "Judah by itself" includes Benjamin, as in 1 Kings 11:32, 11:36, where David's house keeps "one tribe." Excavations show that Jerusalem expanded greatly in the late eighth century BC, spreading onto the western hill, and many scholars connect that growth with refugees from the north after 722. If so, northern traditions came south with them, and later Judah preserved Israel's memory, including perhaps parts of Hosea, Amos and the Elijah and Elisha stories.

a: Even Judah did not keep the commands
p: Kings turns from Israel to Judah in mid-sermon. Many scholars see a later editor writing after Jerusalem fell.
b: 17:19–20 interrupts the account of Israel's sin to say that Judah walked the same road, and "the whole seed of Israel" was rejected. Read in the story's order, it is a warning that Judah could suffer the same fate, as Jeremiah would tell it (Jeremiah 3:6–11). Read as a critical scholar does, it is a note by an exilic editor who already knew of 586. Either way, the fall of Samaria becomes a lesson for Judah, and the reader of the whole book is meant to hear it as such (23:27).

a: For he had torn Israel from David's house
p: The LORD tore the kingdom from Solomon's son (1 Kings 11:31). Kings now traces Israel's end back to that day.
b: Ahijah tore his new cloak into twelve pieces and gave Jeroboam ten, saying, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'Look, I am tearing the kingdom out of Solomon's hand, and I will give the ten tribes to you'" (1 Kings 11:31). The split was God's doing (1 Kings 12:15, 12:24); the calves were Jeroboam's (1 Kings 12:28–30). Kings ends its history of the north by naming both. The verb "pushed away" is spelled two ways in the Hebrew, as "drove away" and "led astray"; both fit.

a: and is there to this day
p: "To this day" begins a long question: did the northern tribes vanish, and will they return?
b: The rabbis disagreed. Rabbi Akiva held that the ten tribes will not return, reading Deuteronomy 29:28, "and flung them into another land, where they are today"; Rabbi Eliezer held that they will (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:3). The prophets promised a reunited Israel (Jeremiah 31:1–20; Ezekiel 37:15–28). The New Testament speaks of "our twelve tribes" and writes to "the twelve tribes in the dispersion" (Acts 26:7; James 1:1). Historians think many northerners were absorbed into the peoples they lived among, some fled to Judah, and many stayed in the land. Several communities, such as the Beta Israel of Ethiopia, have traditions of descent from the ten tribes. See the topic "The Lost Tribes of Israel."
r: Deuteronomy 29:28; Jeremiah 31:1–20; Ezekiel 37:15–28; Acts 26:7; James 1:1; Revelation 7:4–8

a: Then the king of Assyria brought in people
t: Where did the Samaritans come from?
p: Jewish tradition took this passage as the origin of the Samaritans. The Samaritans tell a very different story.
b: Josephus calls the Samaritans "Cuthaeans," after Cuthah, and says they claimed kinship with the Jews only when it suited them (Antiquities 9.288–291); the rabbis also called them Kutim. The Samaritans themselves say they are Shamerim, "keepers" of the Law, descendants of Ephraim and Manasseh who never left the land, and that the schism began when Eli moved the sanctuary from Mount Gerizim to Shiloh, as told in their chronicles. Most historians today think both sides simplify: some northern Israelites remained after 722 (2 Chronicles 30:1–11; 2 Kings 23:15–20), some foreigners were settled, and the decisive split between Samaritans and Jews came much later, in the Persian and Hellenistic periods, around the temple on Gerizim. Genetic studies find Samaritan family lines close to other Israelite populations.

a: from Babylon, from Cuthah, from Avva, from Hamath and Sepharvaim
p: Assyria moved conquered peoples both ways. Babylon, Cuthah and Hamath were all subdued by Sargon II.
b: Assyria broke up rebellious nations by trading their populations. Sargon fought Babylon (710 BC) and crushed Hamath (720 BC). Cuthah (Tell Ibrahim) was a city near Babylon, the cult center of Nergal (17:30). Avva may be the Ivvah of 18:34; Sepharvaim may be a town in Syria (perhaps the Sibraim of Ezekiel 47:16) rather than Babylonian Sippar. Sargon's records also tell of Arab tribes settled in Samaria about 715 BC, and Ezra mentions later settlers brought by Esarhaddon and "Osnappar," probably Ashurbanipal (Ezra 4:2, 4:10).

a: the LORD sent the lions in among them
p: Lions still lived in the land then. Later rabbis called the Samaritans "lion converts."
b: Lions are mentioned often in the Israel of this period (1 Kings 13:24; 1 Kings 20:36), and a land emptied of its farmers would be quickly taken over by wild animals, as the Law warns (Exodus 23:29; Leviticus 26:22). The newcomers read the lions as the anger of the local god, an ordinary belief in their world. Kings agrees that it was the LORD's doing. The Talmud records a debate whether the Samaritans were "lion converts" (gerei arayot), who adopted Israel's God only out of fear, or true converts (Bavli Kiddushin 75b).

a: the ways of the god of the land
p: The Assyrians assume each land has its own god with his own rules. Mishpat here means his customary worship.
b: Mishpat, often "justice" or "ruling," here means the proper way, the custom, as in Samuel's warning about "the ways of the king who will rule them" (1 Samuel 8:9; the same word in 1 Samuel 8:11). Ancient peoples believed gods were bound to their lands: Aram thought the LORD was a god of the hills (1 Kings 20:23), and Naaman took two mule-loads of Israel's soil home to worship the LORD in Damascus (5:17). The irony is that the LORD of Israel is the God of the whole earth, yet he will now be worshiped in Samaria as one god among many.

a: came and settled in Bethel
p: The priest who teaches the newcomers settles at Bethel, home of Jeroboam's calf.
b: Bethel was where Jeroboam set up a gold calf and a priesthood not from Levi (1 Kings 12:29–33), and where an unnamed man of God foretold Josiah's destruction of its altar (1 Kings 13:1–3), fulfilled in 23:15–20. A priest of that northern sanctuary teaching "how to fear the LORD" helps explain the mixed religion that follows. Some scholars think he taught a genuine Israelite form of worship that later became Samaritan practice.

a: the people of Samaria
t: The only "Samaritans" in the Hebrew Bible
p: Hashomronim occurs only here. It means Samaria's former Israelite people, not the later Samaritans.
b: The KJV translates "the Samaritans," which suggests the later religious community of the New Testament. In context, the "people of Samaria" are the Israelites who had built the high places before they were deported; the new settlers put their own gods in those shrines. The Samaritans of later history call themselves not Shomronim but Shamerim, "keepers" of the Law, and they deny that this verse is about them.

a: Succoth-benoth
p: Some of these gods are known from Mesopotamia and Syria. The Talmud gave each an animal form.
b: Nergal was the god of plague and the underworld, worshiped at Cuthah. Succoth-benoth ("booths of daughters" in Hebrew) may be a distorted form of a Babylonian name, perhaps Zarpanitu, Marduk's consort. Ashima may be the "Ashimah of Samaria" by which Amos says people swore (Amos 8:14), and a god called Ashim-Bethel appears among Jews at Elephantine in Egypt. Nibhaz and Tartak are unknown. The Talmud said Succoth-benoth was worshiped as a hen, Nergal as a rooster, Ashima as a goat, Nibhaz as a dog and Tartak as a donkey (Bavli Sanhedrin 63b). Verdict: real gods of real places, some names garbled or mocked in transmission.

a: Adrammelech and Anammelech
p: The names may be Adad-milki and Anu-milki, or "Adad is king" and "Anat is king." Their worshipers burned children.
b: "Melech" means king, and the names may stand for the storm god Adad and the sky god Anu (or the goddess Anat) as "king." Child sacrifice by fire is condemned in Israel's law (Deuteronomy 12:31; Deuteronomy 18:10) and in 17:17, but these settlers bring the practice with them. A son of Sennacherib with the name Adrammelech appears in 19:37. The link between these names and the Molech of Leviticus 18:21 is debated.

a: They do not fear the LORD
t: Do they fear the LORD or not?
p: 17:32–33 and 17:41 say the settlers "feared the LORD"; 17:34 says they do not. The answer depends on what "fear" means.
b: To "fear" (yare') the LORD can mean to worship him in form or to be wholly loyal to him. The settlers feared the LORD in the first sense and also served their gods; in the second sense they did not fear him at all, since fearing the LORD means fearing no other gods (17:35–39). Some scholars think 17:34–40 is a separate piece aimed at the exiled Israelites, "the sons of Jacob," or at Judah, and that 17:41 returns to the settlers. Elijah's question still stands over the passage: "How long will you limp along on two crutches?" (1 Kings 18:21).

a: the sons of Jacob, the one he named Israel
p: The narrator reaches back to Genesis, where God gave Jacob the name Israel.
b: God renamed Jacob "Israel" at the Jabbok and again at Bethel (Genesis 32:28; Genesis 35:10). Elijah used the same words when he built the altar on Carmel with twelve stones for "the Jacob the LORD had spoken to, saying, 'Israel will be your name'" (1 Kings 18:31). At the end of the northern kingdom, Kings reminds readers that the name belonged to all twelve tribes and came with a covenant.

a: with great strength and with an arm stretched out
p: Deuteronomy's usual phrase is "a strong hand and an outstretched arm." Kings has "great strength."
b: Deuteronomy describes the exodus as done "with a strong hand and an outstretched arm" (Deuteronomy 5:15; Deuteronomy 26:8). Kings, like Moses' prayer "by your great power and your outstretched arm" (Deuteronomy 9:29) and Jeremiah 32:17, uses "great strength" (the same Hebrew word, koach). The covenant of 17:35–39 is a summary of the first two of the Ten Words: no other gods, no bowing to images (Exodus 20:3–5; Deuteronomy 5:7–9).

a: Their sons and their sons' sons are still doing what their fathers did, to this day
t: "To this day": when was this written?
p: The writer looks back on generations of mixed worship in Samaria, so this ending was written long after 722.
b: "Their sons and their sons' sons" implies at least two generations after the settlement. Traditional readers date the passage to the prophetic historian of the late monarchy or exile. Critical scholars often see 17:24–41 as growing in stages, with sharp polemic added in the Persian period, when Jerusalem's leaders refused the help of "the people of the land" (Ezra 4:1–4). Read today, the passage is a Judean account of northern neighbors. The Samaritans, who still worship at Mount Gerizim, read it as a hostile story about other people.
